newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italy back in EU currency fold - after a fight.
newsitem.headline: Italy back in EU currency fold - after a fight.

text.p: Italy, unceremoniously dumped from the European Union's currency grid four years ago, has returned to the bloc's currency fold, but only after EU partners make clear they have no time for weak currencies.

Two days of hard bargaining in Brussels culminated late on Sunday night with an agreement by EU finance ministers and central bank governors to let the lira rejoin the exchange rate mechanism (ERM) at a central rate of 990 lira to the mark.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi hailed the move as a "fundamental step" towards Italy being a founder member of the EU's single currency in 1999.
"To have brought the lira into Europe is the consequence of the seriousness of our economic policy and the stability we have given the country," he was reported as saying by Italy's ANSA news agency.
Being part of the ERM, a grid designed to keep currencies stable, is one criteria for qualifying for the single currency, the Euro.
But the re-entry of the lira -- thrown out of the ERM in 1992 amid ferocious market speculation -- only came after a fight.

Italy sought to enter at a rate no stronger than 1,000 lira to the mark. Its partners, however, would have nothing of it, fearful both of the damage a weak lira could do to their trade and of encouraging a weak currency to qualify for the Euro.
Officials said few, if any, EU countries were willing to let the lira in at a rate of 1,000 lira. Some were talking in terms of 950 to 980 lira to the mark.

Rome's partners said the strong rate matched Italy's new-found economic status and boosted its credibility. A statement congratulated Italy on the "substantial adjustment" its economy had already made as EU countries try to prepare for the Euro.

But senior officials from Germany and the Netherlands, part of the likely hard core of Euro countries, also made it clear that Italy was not being invited to join the single currency simply by being allowed back into the ERM.
"It is certainly not a comment on Italy's qualification for monetary union," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said after the meeting.
A fast growing view on financial markets that countries such as Italy, Spain and Portugal with relatively weak economies could qualify for the single currency has sent shivers through the Bundesbank.
This has been exacerbated by one-off budget moves, such as Italy's planned Euro-tax, which some officials see as thinly disguised fiscal trickery to meet the Euro qualifications.
Italy's re-entry into the ERM leaves only three of the 15 EU countries outside the grid -- Sweden, Britain and Greece.
Neither Sweden or Britain believe that being in the ERM is a necessary step to the single currency -- which they are anyway dubious about.
Sweden said on Sunday Italy's move would have no effect on its position. Any suggestion by Britain that it might want to enter would trigger a huge Euro war in Britain's ruling Conservative Party.
Greece's economy is too weak to be considered a candidate for either the ERM or the single currency.
